parsed_response.reasoning: The diff confirms the factual core: Calendar.d.ts changes the interface to `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number)` while LarkCalendarService (`async createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)`) and Office365CalendarService (`async createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)`) keep single-parameter signatures, so TypeScript genuinely will not flag them (functions with fewer params are assignable to the interface slot). The finding's bivariance mechanism is slightly imprecise (fewer-parameter assignability, not bivariance per se), but the observable claim — the new credentialId contract is not enforced on these implementers, so per-credential destinationCalendar selection (as implemented in GoogleCalendarService via `cal.credentialId === credentialId`) is silently unsupported there — is accurate and grounded in the diff. This is not a behavioral regression (Lark/Office365 fall back to the first destination calendar, matching prior single-object behavior), so it's not a bug; it is a specific, decision-relevant API-contract consistency concern a maintainer should weigh when shipping the multi-destination-calendar refactor.

judged_text: packages/types/Calendar.d.ts:221 — `Calendar.createEvent` gained a required `credentialId: number` second parameter, but TypeScript's bivariant method-parameter checking lets `LarkCalendarService`/`Office365CalendarService`, which still declare `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)`, satisfy `implements Calendar` without a compile error, so the interface contract silently fails to enforce the very capability (per-credential calendar selection) the signature change was meant to guarantee (P2, confidence 80).
